title: Notification service
like: the service that sends every push, email and text
brief: Every other team asks you to send messages: order shipped, new login, a sale starting. You send them by push, email and text through outside providers who have their own limits. Send each message once, and never block the team that asked.

clarify.q: Does the sender wait until the message is delivered?
clarify.a: No. They only need to know it was accepted. Delivery happens afterwards.

clarify.q: What if the same message is asked for twice?
clarify.a: Send it only once. A double "your card was charged" text is a bad day.
A few minutes is fine for marketing, and up to half an hour while a provider is down; later than that it counts as failed. Login codes need seconds.
Yes. Check their preferences before every send.

notes: Providers cap how fast you may send: push ≈ 10,000/s, email ≈ 1,000/s, text ≈ 100/s (approx.).
Texts cost far more than email or push.

numbers.label: Messages to send per second at peak
Messages per day
numbers.how: Average load is about 0.4 of peak: 5,600 × 0.4 × 86,400 ≈ 190 million (approx.)

numbers.label: Email sending limit
numbers.how: The provider cap in this scenario: you must spread load across channels and wait politely (approx.)

hints: The team asking should not wait for the message to go out. What can hold the work?
Put a queue between asking and sending. Check for duplicates and preferences while sending.
Gateway, servers, queue, workers that check an idempotency store and consent, then push, email and text providers. Add a dead-letter queue for bad messages.

editorial.summary: Accept the request, store it in a queue and answer quickly. Workers pull from the queue at a speed the providers allow, check that the message was not already sent and that the person agreed, then send. The queue absorbs bursts and outages.

designs.name: Queue, idempotent workers, push and email
designs.why: The queue soaks up a campaign blast. An idempotency check makes retries safe. The reference uses two providers: push at about 10,000 sends/s and email at about 1,000 sends/s. One slowing or failing does not stop the other. Text delivery would need a separate SMS provider capped at about 100 sends/s, with its own queue and cost budget (approx.).

tradeoffs: A queue makes sending late but never lost. Without one, a slow provider slows every sender.
At-least-once delivery plus an idempotency check gives "once" in practice and costs one extra lookup per message.
Spreading across channels increases resilience but multiplies the number of limits you must respect.
A dead-letter queue keeps one bad message from blocking all the rest.
editorial.realWorld: Big apps send billions of notifications a day. Push is nearly free, email is about $0.10 per thousand, and a text costs several cents each (approx.).

correctness.prompt: A worker sends a message, then crashes before recording success. What key and delivery states would you store so a retry does not send it twice?
correctness.discussion: Give each logical message a stable key, scoped to its recipient and channel, and enforce a unique constraint on that key. Save the request and an outbox entry in one transaction, then track pending, sending and delivered states. A queue alone does not prevent duplicates. If the provider accepts the send but the worker crashes, retry with the same provider idempotency key or query its status. Without provider support, exactly-once external delivery cannot be guaranteed: discuss whether a possible duplicate or a possible missed message is acceptable.

fields.label: Retry key
options: A new key for each delivery attempt
One stable message, recipient and channel key
fields.explanation: Retries must reuse the logical message key, scoped to recipient and channel, with durable uniqueness.

fields.label: Provider accepted, worker crashed
options: Retry with the same provider key or query its status
Send again because local success is missing
fields.explanation: Reconcile the unknown outcome with provider idempotency or a status query. Without provider support, exactly-once external delivery cannot be guaranteed.

correctness.limits: The traffic score does not verify key scope, atomic outbox writes or exactly-once delivery at an external provider.
